8730:
An inexactitude is a statement, claim, or piece of information that is not fully accurate, precise, or correct — something that misses the mark of truth, either a little or a lot.

Think of it this way: imagine you are drawing a circle freehand. It's roughly a circle, but not a perfect one. That gap between what it is and what it's supposed to be — that's the spirit of an inexactitude.
Two Ways the Word Is Used

The word works in two distinct ways, and both are important.

1. As a "thing" — a specific faulty statement

Here, an inexactitude is a concrete piece of information that is wrong, misleading, or imprecise. It's a countable use of the word, meaning you can have one inexactitude or many inexactitudes.

"His report was full of inexactitudes — wrong dates, inflated numbers, and misquoted facts."

Each inexactitude here is a specific, identifiable error in what was said or written.

2. As a quality or condition — the state of being inexact

Here, the word describes an overall lack of precision or accuracy, not one specific mistake but a general sloppiness with the truth or the facts.

"The inexactitude of her memory made it hard to rely on her account of events."

She's not necessarily lying — her memory is just fuzzy and imprecise.
The Tone of the Word — This Is Crucial

This is where inexactitude really becomes interesting and useful. The word carries a distinctly formal, sophisticated, and often deliberately gentle tone. It is the kind of word a diplomat, a lawyer, a professor, or a careful writer reaches for.

When someone uses inexactitude instead of blunter words like "mistake," "error," or "lie," they are usually doing one of two things:

  • Being polite or tactful — softening the blow of calling something wrong
  • Being sarcastically restrained — making the accusation sound civilised on the surface while the sting is still very much there

This makes it a powerful word. It lets the speaker maintain an air of calm and sophistication while still making a sharp point.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are all in the same neighbourhood, but they are not identical:

Error / Mistake — A neutral, everyday word for something that is simply wrong. No special tone. A child can make an error. A machine can make an error.

Inaccuracy — Also means something not accurate. Very close to inexactitude, but slightly more clinical and direct. An inaccuracy feels like a measured, factual observation.

Imprecision — Focuses specifically on vagueness or lack of detail. Something imprecise is blurry or loosely stated, not necessarily false.

Inexactitude — Carries more weight and formality than all of the above. It implies a degree of deliberate care in choosing the word, which itself signals something. When someone calls your statement an inexactitude rather than a mistake, they are being precise about your imprecision — and that contrast is often intentional.

Lie — A deliberate untruth. Inexactitude is sometimes used as a refined euphemism for a lie, which brings us to the most famous use of this word.
The Most Famous Use of This Word

The word inexactitude became immortal through a remark by Winston Churchill. When accused in the British Parliament of misleading the House, rather than admit to lying, he responded by referring to his statement as a "terminological inexactitude."

In plain English, that phrase means: "a lie" — but said in the most elaborate, dignified, and technically deniable way imaginable.

This is perhaps the most elegant illustration of what the word can do. It wraps an uncomfortable truth in a velvet glove.

• "The witness's testimony contained several inexactitudes that the lawyer quickly exposed."

(Specific wrong or misleading statements in what the witness said.)

  • "The professor was known for the inexactitude of his lecture notes — details were always a bit off."

(A general condition of being loose and imprecise with facts.)

  • "Let's call it an inexactitude rather than a lie, since I'm not sure she knew she was wrong."

(Using the word deliberately to be charitable — she may have been imprecise rather than dishonest.)

  • "His budget forecast was riddled with inexactitudes, and nobody caught them until it was too late."

(Multiple specific errors in numbers or projections.)
The Single Sentence to Carry With You

If you want one sentence to lock in the meaning forever, here it is:

An inexactitude is a formal, sophisticated word for something said or written that is not fully accurate — ranging from a small imprecision to what is, in polite terms, a lie.

What it isA statement, fact, or quality that lacks full accuracy or precision
ToneFormal, polished, sometimes euphemistic or sarcastically restrained
Can meanA specific wrong claim, OR the general state of being imprecise
Closest cousinsInaccuracy, imprecision — but more elevated in register
Used whenYou want to point out something is wrong without being blunt, or when you want to sound precise and authoritative
8731:
Something is inexcusable when it is so wrong, so harmful, or so unacceptable that no reason, explanation, or excuse can make it okay.

Think of it this way: when someone does something bad, we sometimes say "well, they had a reason" or "I understand why they did it" — and that softens our judgment. But when something is inexcusable, even a good reason won't save you. The action is simply beyond defense.

The word is built from two parts: "in-" (meaning not) + "excusable" (meaning able to be excused or forgiven). Put them together: not able to be excused. Period.

This is not a neutral word. It carries strong moral weight and disapproval. When someone calls something inexcusable, they are not just saying "this was bad." They are saying:

  • This crosses a clear line.
  • The person responsible should be fully held accountable.
  • There is nothing — no circumstances, no pressure, no story — that reduces the wrongness of this.

It is the verbal equivalent of slamming a door shut on any attempt to justify what happened.
What Kinds of Things Are Called Inexcusable?

The word is used for actions, behavior, mistakes, or treatment that are judged to be beyond forgiveness or justification. Here are natural, everyday examples:

  • "His rudeness toward the elderly woman was inexcusable."

(No matter how stressed he was, speaking to her that way was simply not okay.)

  • "The doctor's negligence was inexcusable — the patient could have died."

(A doctor has a duty of care; nothing justifies abandoning it.)

  • "Forgetting your best friend's wedding is inexcusable."

(There is really no good excuse for that level of neglect.)

  • "The delays in sending aid to the disaster victims were inexcusable."

(People were suffering; no bureaucratic reason is acceptable here.)

Notice in every case: there is a clear standard of what should have been done, and the action (or inaction) fell so far below that standard that no excuse holds up.

Very strong. You would not call a minor mistake inexcusable. If you accidentally spill someone's coffee, that is a mistake — not inexcusable. But if a nurse gives a patient the wrong medicine despite clear warnings, and the patient is harmed — that is inexcusable.

Reserve this word for situations where:

  1. A person had a clear responsibility or knew what was right.
  2. They failed badly — through action or inaction.
  3. No reasonable explanation can reduce the gravity of what they did.

These synonyms help you understand the word by seeing its family:

  • Unforgivable — cannot be forgiven (slightly more emotional and personal)
  • Unpardonable — cannot be pardoned (more formal, often moral or legal)
  • Indefensible — cannot be defended with any argument
  • Unjustifiable — no justification exists for it

Among these, inexcusable is the most commonly used in everyday speech and writing.

The opposite of inexcusable is excusable — meaning the behavior can be understood or forgiven given the circumstances.

  • "Spilling water on the keyboard was excusable — you didn't see it there."
  • "Deliberately destroying someone's work is inexcusable."

You can also use justifiable, forgivable, understandable, or pardonable as opposites.

The word is often strengthened with adverbs:

  • "absolutely inexcusable"
  • "simply inexcusable"
  • "completely inexcusable"
  • "utterly inexcusable"

These reinforce that there is zero room for any excuse.
Tone and Register: When Do People Use It?

This word sounds formal to semi-formal. You will hear it from:

  • Teachers criticizing a student's dishonesty.
  • Managers addressing serious workplace misconduct.
  • Judges or lawyers describing harmful actions.
  • Journalists or commentators reacting to failures by people in power.
  • Everyday people when something genuinely outrages them.

You would not use it in casual small talk. If your friend is five minutes late, you would not say "This is inexcusable." — that would sound over-dramatic. But if a surgeon left a patient on the operating table to take a personal call, inexcusable fits perfectly.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

Inexcusable = So wrong that no excuse, explanation, or reason can make it acceptable.

When you call something inexcusable, you are closing the door on all defense. You are saying the act stands condemned, fully and finally, on its own.
8732:
Something is inexhaustible when it cannot be used up, no matter how much you draw from it. It keeps going. It keeps giving. You cannot drain it dry.

Think of a magic well. You lower a bucket every single day, pull it up full of water, and yet the well is never empty. The next day — full again. The day after — still full. That well would be inexhaustible.

The simplest version: so vast, powerful, or constantly renewed that it will never run out.
The Key Idea That Makes This Word Special

The word is not just about something being large or plentiful. A very large tank of water is big and plentiful, but it is not inexhaustible — keep taking from it, and eventually it will be empty.

Inexhaustible is stronger than that. It means that the emptying never comes. You could keep taking, keep using, keep testing it — and still find more. The supply resists being finished. That resistance is the heart of the word.

Literally, it describes a real physical resource that genuinely does not run out. Sunlight is often described as an inexhaustible energy source — the sun keeps producing heat and light without ever being depleted by our use of it. An underground spring that flows without stopping, year after year, is inexhaustible.

Figuratively — and this is how the word is used most often — it describes a quality in a person, like energy, patience, or curiosity, that appears to have no limit. The person simply never runs out of it. A nurse who stays calm and caring after a 14-hour shift, and then comes back tomorrow and does it again, has inexhaustible compassion. A child who keeps asking "why?" after every single answer you give has inexhaustible curiosity.
What Kinds of Things Are Called Inexhaustible?

Certain ideas naturally go with this word. Here are the most common:

Inexhaustible energy or stamina — a person who never seems to get tired, no matter how hard they work.

Inexhaustible patience — a person who stays calm and tolerant no matter how many times they are tested.

Inexhaustible curiosity — a mind that is always hungry for more knowledge, never satisfied, never bored.

Inexhaustible enthusiasm or passion — a person whose excitement about something never fades, even after years.

Inexhaustible creativity — someone who keeps producing fresh, original ideas without ever running dry.

Inexhaustible supply or source — a reserve of something (knowledge, money, talent, material) that keeps providing without end.

"Despite working sixteen hours a day, she had an inexhaustible drive that kept her going."
→ No matter how exhausting the work, her determination never ran out.

"The ocean once seemed inexhaustible, but overfishing has proven otherwise."
→ People used to believe the ocean's fish supply would never run out — but it can, and it has.

"He was an inexhaustible conversationalist — every topic led to another story, another question, another idea."
→ His ability to keep a conversation alive never seemed to run dry.

"Children's questions are often inexhaustible — answer one, and three more appear."
→ The questions keep coming with no sign of stopping.

"Great literature is an inexhaustible source of wisdom — you can return to it your whole life and keep finding new meaning."
→ No matter how many times you read it, it keeps giving you something new.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Inexhaustible almost always carries a sense of admiration or wonder. When you call something inexhaustible, you are impressed by it. You are marveling at its endurance, its abundance, its refusal to quit. It is a word that celebrates limitlessness.

However, it can also appear in a cautionary or sobering way — to challenge a dangerous assumption. "No resource is truly inexhaustible" is a powerful statement. It warns people not to take abundance for granted.
An Important Nuance: Truly vs. Seemingly Inexhaustible

In everyday use, inexhaustible often means seemingly without end, rather than literally infinite. When someone says a person has inexhaustible energy, they do not mean that person is superhuman. They mean the energy is so great, so impressive, that it appears boundless. The word captures the experience of encountering something that just keeps going — the feeling that no matter how much you use, there is always more where that came from.

It does not mean simply "a lot" or "enough." It is not about abundance alone. It is about abundance that cannot be drained. The idea of depletion is built into the word — and inexhaustible is the rejection of that idea. The moment something can, in theory, be fully used up, it is not truly inexhaustible.
A Simple Image to Lock It In

Picture a candle that never burns down. You light it, it gives you warmth and light for hours — and yet when you look at it, it is as tall as it was when you started. You could burn it for a thousand years and it would never melt away.

That candle is inexhaustible.

Now picture a person's kindness that works the same way — no matter how much is given away, no matter how many people it touches or how many difficult days test it, it is always full again. That is what it means to say someone's kindness is inexhaustible.

That is the complete picture of the word. One sentence to carry with you: inexhaustible means it cannot be used up, no matter how hard or how long you try.
8733:
"Inexorable" describes something — or someone — that cannot be stopped, changed, or persuaded, no matter what. It is completely and absolutely unstoppable. More than that, it is also unmoved by any appeal. You can beg it, argue with it, reason with it, cry in front of it — and it will not respond. It simply continues.

Think of a massive boulder rolling down a hill. Nothing in its path can stop it. It doesn't speed up out of anger or slow down out of sympathy. It just rolls forward, indifferent to everything. That boulder is inexorable.
The two ways the word is used

When describing a force or process, "inexorable" means it is impossible to prevent or interrupt. It is ongoing, continuous, and will not be halted.

"The inexorable rise of sea levels is reshaping coastlines around the world."
"The disease spread with inexorable speed, overwhelming every hospital."
"Time is inexorable — it does not pause for anyone."

When describing a person, "inexorable" means they cannot be softened or persuaded by emotional appeals. They will not bend, no matter what.

"The inexorable judge refused every plea for mercy."
"She was inexorable — no amount of explaining or begging changed her decision."

Both uses share the same heart: nothing gets through. Nothing makes it stop or change.
The feeling and weight of the word

"Inexorable" is a serious, formal, heavyweight word. It is not used for small or trivial things. You would never say "the inexorable loss of my phone charger" — that would sound ridiculous. But you would absolutely say "the inexorable decline of a civilization" or "the inexorable advance of old age."

The word almost always carries a sense of gravity, awe, or even dread. When something is described as inexorable, the message being sent is: this is bigger than you, and there is nothing you can do about it. It often appears in writing about history, nature, death, fate, science, or time — things that operate on a scale beyond individual human control.
The key idea hidden inside the word

The thing that makes "inexorable" special — and different from just saying "unstoppable" — is its built-in indifference. An inexorable force doesn't merely overcome resistance. It doesn't even register resistance. It is completely cold and unresponsive to pleas, obstacles, or opposition. It doesn't hear you.

This is why the word is so powerful when applied to people. Calling someone "inexorable" doesn't just mean they're stubborn. It means specifically that your emotional appeals have zero effect on them. A stubborn person at least wrestles with your plea. An inexorable person doesn't even flinch.
How it compares to similar words

Inevitable tells you that something will happen. "Inexorable" goes further — it tells you the thing is already in motion, continuously moving forward, and cannot be interrupted at any point along the way.

Relentless emphasizes that something never pauses or shows mercy. "Inexorable" emphasizes that it cannot be stopped or reasoned with — the focus is on the impossibility of halting it, not just its pace.

Unyielding means refusing to give way. When applied to a person, "inexorable" is more specific — it means refusing to yield to persuasion or emotional appeals in particular.

Unstoppable is the closest everyday synonym, but it is casual and flat. "Inexorable" adds formality, grandeur, and a sense of something vast and inevitable — it sounds like something a philosopher or a historian would write, not something you'd say about a running back in football.

In real writing, you'll frequently see "inexorable" paired with particular words. The most common are:

"The inexorable march of time" — time moving forward no matter what anyone does.
"The inexorable logic of an argument" — a chain of reasoning that leads unavoidably to one conclusion.
"Inexorable decline" or "inexorable rise" — a long, unstoppable downward or upward movement.
"With inexorable force" or "with inexorable certainty" — emphasizing that something is happening with absolute, unbreakable momentum.
The single sentence to remember it forever

If you remember one thing: inexorable = cannot be stopped, and cannot be moved by any appeal.

Unstoppable + coldly indifferent to all resistance. That's the whole word.
8734:
"Inexorably" means in a way that cannot be stopped, slowed down, or changed — no matter what anyone does.

When something happens inexorably, it moves forward with total, absolute certainty. No force, no plea, no action can prevent it or alter its course. It will happen. It is happening. Nothing can get in the way.

This word actually carries three ideas at once, stacked on top of each other:

1. It cannot be stopped.
Whatever is moving inexorably will reach its destination or conclusion. There is no wall you can build, no button you can press, no escape route you can take.

2. It cannot be persuaded or begged.
This is a subtle but important layer. "Inexorably" has an ancient sense of something that won't respond to pleading, arguing, or prayer. Imagine begging the ocean not to rise — it doesn't listen, because it can't listen. That indifference to human appeal is baked into this word.

3. It is relentless — it never pauses.
It doesn't rest, hesitate, or slow down. It keeps going with a steady, grinding continuity.

Put all three together: something inexorable is unstoppable, unpersuadable, and tireless — all at once.

"Inexorably" is not a neutral word. It carries weight and gravity. When a writer uses it, they are signaling that something serious and large is at work — something bigger than any individual's ability to fight it.

It often comes with a quiet sense of dread, awe, or solemnity. It's the feeling you get watching a glacier slowly crushing everything in its path — massive, cold, and utterly indifferent to whatever stands before it.

Read these slowly and feel how the word works in each one:

  • "Time moves inexorably forward."

You cannot pause time, reverse it, or negotiate with it. It advances without mercy or interruption.

  • "The disease progressed inexorably, despite every treatment the doctors tried."

Nothing slowed it down. Medicine, willpower, prayers — none of it worked. It kept going.

  • "The small town was inexorably changing as the city grew around it."

Nobody may have wanted the change. People may have resisted it. But it happened anyway, steadily and completely.

  • "He was inexorably drawn toward the one decision he had been trying to avoid his whole life."

No matter how hard he tried to escape it, something kept pulling him back. The outcome felt sealed.

  • "History inexorably punishes nations that ignore the suffering of their people."

The consequence is certain. It cannot be dodged or bargained away.

Notice that in every example, resistance is futile. That's the essence of the word.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words feel close to "inexorably," but they are not the same:

"Inevitably" tells you the outcome is certain — it will happen. "Inexorably" tells you the process of getting there cannot be stopped either. "Inevitably" is about the destination. "Inexorably" is about the unstoppable journey toward it. Often they overlap, but "inexorably" is more vivid — it paints the picture of something actively, relentlessly moving forward.

"Relentlessly" means without rest or mercy — something keeps going and going. But it doesn't carry the sense of being impossible to stop or change. A person can relentlessly work hard, but someone could technically stop them. Something happening inexorably cannot be stopped, period.

"Steadily" just means at a constant, even pace. It's completely neutral — no sense of being unstoppable, no gravity, no weight. "The rain fell steadily" is calm and ordinary. "The floodwaters rose inexorably" is ominous and final.

"Unstoppably" is the closest cousin — it captures the "cannot be halted" idea well. But it's a more casual, blunter word. "Inexorably" is more formal, literary, and layered. It also carries that extra shade of "unpersuadable" that "unstoppably" lacks.
Where You Will See This Word

"Inexorably" is a formal, serious, literary word. You will find it in:

  • Literary novels and serious fiction
  • Historical writing and biographies
  • Quality journalism covering major events
  • Academic writing
  • Powerful speeches

You would not say it casually to a friend. Nobody says "I inexorably made my way to the fridge." It would sound strange. The word belongs to serious, weighty contexts — discussions of time, history, nature, fate, decline, progress, or death.
A Simple Test for When It Fits

Before using "inexorably," ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is what I'm describing something that genuinely cannot be stopped or changed?
  2. Is it moving forward with relentless, continuous force?
  3. Is the tone of what I'm writing serious and weighty?

If all three answers are yes, "inexorably" fits perfectly.
If you had to carry just one idea in your pocket: "inexorably" means in a way that moves forward with complete, unstoppable certainty — indifferent to any attempt to slow it, stop it, or change it.
8735:
Something is inexpedient when it is not a wise or practical choice in a given situation — not because it is morally wrong or forbidden, but because it simply will not work out well, will cause problems, or will go against your own interests given the current circumstances.

The simplest way to understand it: a bad move, not because of ethics, but because of practicality.

The central question that "inexpedient" asks is: "Is this a smart thing to do right now, given the situation?"

If the answer is no — if doing it would likely backfire, create unnecessary trouble, or get in the way of your goals — then it is inexpedient.

Notice what the word is not about:

  • It is not about whether something is morally right or wrong.
  • It is not about whether something is legal or illegal.
  • It is not about whether something is possible or impossible.

It is about:

  • Whether an action is well-suited to the current circumstances.
  • Whether the timing, approach, or method is sensible.
  • Whether doing it will actually help you achieve your goal — or hurt you.

Example 1: "It would be inexpedient to raise prices during a recession."
Raising prices is not a crime. But during a recession, when people are already struggling financially, doing so would drive customers away and hurt the business. The circumstances make it a poor practical decision.

Example 2: "She found it inexpedient to argue with her boss right before a performance review."
Arguing with your boss is not forbidden. But the timing makes it a bad idea — it could seriously harm your chances of a good review. The situation makes the action work against you.

Example 3: "The general considered it inexpedient to attack without proper supplies."
An attack is not wrong in the context of a battle, but launching one without the right supplies is practically unwise — it would put the army at a disadvantage. The circumstances make it a poor move.

In all three examples, the action itself is not the problem. The problem is the mismatch between the action and the situation.
A Subtle but Important Point: "Even If It Seems Right"

One of the most interesting things about "inexpedient" is that it can apply even to actions that seem good or correct in theory.

For example, being completely blunt and honest with someone might be the morally "right" thing to do. But if that bluntness will only cause conflict, shut down a conversation, and achieve nothing useful — it becomes inexpedient. It is not the wrong thing to do in a moral sense; it is just the wrong move for the situation.

This is what separates "inexpedient" from words like "wrong" or "immoral." It lives purely in the world of practical judgment, not moral judgment.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Unwise — Very close in feel, but "unwise" is more general and refers broadly to poor judgment. "Inexpedient" is more specific: it zeroes in on whether something fits the particular situation or goal at hand.

Inadvisable — Also very similar, and in fact the closest synonym. The slight difference is that "inadvisable" simply means "not recommended," while "inexpedient" carries a stronger sense that the action will actively work against you or the circumstances.

Inappropriate — "Inappropriate" usually means something violates social norms or standards of decency. "Inexpedient" has nothing to do with social norms; it is strictly about practical outcomes.

Impractical — "Impractical" often means something is too difficult or unrealistic to actually carry out. "Inexpedient" means the action is possible, but doing it would be unwise given the situation.

"Inexpedient" is not a mild word. It is not saying something is merely "a little inconvenient" or "slightly awkward." It signals that the course of action would be noticeably damaging to your goals, interests, or situation. When someone calls something inexpedient, they are making a clear, deliberate judgment: this should not be done, here, now, in this way.
Register: Where You'll See This Word

"Inexpedient" is a formal word. You are far more likely to encounter it in:

  • Political or government writing ("The committee deemed the measure inexpedient at this time.")
  • Legal or official documents
  • Classic literature and philosophy
  • Formal speeches or essays

In everyday spoken language, people tend to say "not a good idea," "unwise," "a bad move," or "not the right time" — all of which can express the same idea less formally.
If you ever need to recall the word quickly, remember this: inexpedient means "not a good idea in practice, given the current situation." It is always about circumstances, never about morality.
8736:
Something is inexpensive when it does not cost a lot of money. Its price is low.

That's the simple definition. But to truly understand this word, you need to know what makes it different from words that seem similar.

This is where most learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Both words describe a low price. But they carry very different feelings:

"Cheap" has two sides:

  1. It can simply mean a low price ("I bought it cheap.")
  2. But very often, it suggests poor quality — that something is badly made, flimsy, or not worth your time. Calling a product "cheap" is often an insult. Calling a person cheap means they are stingy and avoid spending money even when they should.

"Inexpensive" describes only the price — it says nothing negative about quality. In fact, it quietly hints that something is a good deal: the price is low, but the thing itself is still decent or even good.

A street food stall might serve inexpensive meals — low price, but delicious and filling.

Calling those same meals cheap might suggest they are bad or made with poor ingredients.

So: inexpensive = low price, with no insult attached.

This is why you'll often see "inexpensive" used when someone wants to recommend something affordable without making it sound bad. Writers, reviewers, and advertisers use it as a respectful, positive way to talk about low-cost options.
How it differs from other similar words

Affordable means something is within a person's budget — they can manage to pay for it. Affordability depends on who is buying. A ₹5,000 jacket might be affordable to one person and not to another. "Affordable" is personal.

Inexpensive is more about the actual price being low in general — not just relative to one person's income.

A luxury car can be affordable to a millionaire, but it is never inexpensive.

A basic cotton shirt for ₹200 is inexpensive — its price is objectively low.

Economical focuses on efficiency — getting more value per rupee spent, or using less of something (fuel, money, effort). It's about smart use of resources.

An economical car doesn't just have a low price — it uses less fuel, so it costs less to run.

Budget-friendly is a casual, friendly way to say something is suitable for people who don't want to spend much. It's informal and commonly used in everyday speech and marketing.

Inexpensive is slightly more formal and neutral than "budget-friendly," and far more polite than "cheap."
The connotation (the feeling the word carries)

"Inexpensive" has a neutral to slightly positive feeling. It treats the person buying with respect — it doesn't imply they are poor, stingy, or settling for something bad. It simply states that the price is low.

This makes it a very useful and dignified word when:

  • You want to recommend something low-cost without embarrassing anyone.
  • You want to describe a product's price without suggesting poor quality.
  • You're writing or speaking in a somewhat formal or polished way.

"Inexpensive" is an adjective, so it describes a noun (a thing, a place, a person, an experience). It goes either before the noun or after a linking verb (like "is," "was," "seems").

Before a noun:

  • "She bought an inexpensive dress for the wedding."
  • "The city is full of inexpensive restaurants."
  • "They found an inexpensive solution to the problem."

After a linking verb:

  • "This phone is surprisingly inexpensive."
  • "The repairs turned out to be inexpensive."
  • "Eating at home is inexpensive compared to dining out."

• It does not mean free.
  • It does not mean low quality (that's "cheap").
  • It does not mean it's within your personal budget (that's "affordable" — you might still find something inexpensive out of your reach if you have very little money).
  • It does not say the thing is the best value — just that the price is low.
The direct opposite of inexpensive is expensive — meaning something costs a lot of money.
A simple way to remember it

Think of "inexpensive" as the polite, clean word for "low price." No judgment about quality. No judgment about the buyer. Just a simple, respectful statement: this does not cost much.

Whenever you want to say something is affordable or low-priced without any negative tone, "inexpensive" is almost always the right choice.
8737:
Inexpert means not having the skill, knowledge, or experience needed to do something well.

If a person is inexpert at something, they lack the ability to do it with the confidence, precision, or quality that a trained or experienced person would show. The result of their work is usually noticeable — it looks rough, clumsy, or poorly done compared to what a skilled person would produce.

Think of it this way: an expert is someone who has mastered a skill. Inexpert is simply the opposite — someone who has not mastered it.

This is important, because many learners confuse similar-looking words.

Inexpert does not mean:

  • Completely ignorant or clueless (that would be closer to "incompetent" or "ignorant")
  • Lazy or careless (a person can be inexpert even while trying very hard)
  • Stupid (intelligence has nothing to do with it)

An inexpert person may be trying their best — they simply don't have the refined skill yet. The word is about a lack of skill or expertise, not a lack of effort or intelligence.
Who or What Can Be Described as Inexpert?

This is a key part of understanding the word well. "Inexpert" can describe two things:

1. A Person

You can call a person inexpert when they lack skill in a particular area.

"He is an inexpert carpenter — his shelves wobble and the joints don't sit flush."

"She was still inexpert at driving and found parking stressful."

Notice: the word almost always pairs with "at" when describing a person — inexpert at something.

2. An Action, Attempt, or Result

You can also use "inexpert" to describe the way something was done, or the outcome of someone's work.

"It was an inexpert repair — the pipe stopped leaking for a week, then burst again."

"The surgeon performed an inexpert stitch, leaving a jagged scar."

"Her inexpert handling of the situation made things worse."

Here, you're not directly calling the person inexpert — you're calling the action or result inexpert. This is very common in writing.
A Scale to Place the Word

It helps to see where "inexpert" sits among related words, from least skilled to most skilled:

Incompetent → Inexpert → Novice/Amateur → Capable → Skilled → Expert → Master

  • Incompetent suggests someone is so unskilled they fail even at basic tasks — it's a harsher word.
  • Inexpert is milder. It means the skill is simply underdeveloped. The person can do the thing, but not well.
  • Novice or amateur carries a similar meaning but also implies the person is new to it. Inexpert doesn't necessarily mean new — a person can have been doing something for years and still be inexpert at it.

So "inexpert" occupies a specific spot: below competent, above completely incapable.

"Inexpert" is a slightly formal word. You won't hear it as often in everyday casual conversation as you would in writing, formal speech, or professional critique.

When someone uses it, the tone is usually descriptive and objective, not insulting. It states a fact about the level of skill — it doesn't mock. Compare:

  • "That was a clumsy, awful repair." → Critical and emotional
  • "That was an inexpert repair." → Observational, measured, factual

This is why "inexpert" often appears in reviews, reports, professional assessments, and literary writing.

Some words naturally sit beside "inexpert" more often than others:

  • Inexpert handling — most common; used when someone manages or operates something without the needed skill
  • Inexpert attempt — when someone tries to do something but the effort lacks skill
  • Inexpert work / craftsmanship — the result is poor in quality due to lack of skill
  • Inexpert advice — guidance given without proper knowledge
  • Inexpert eye — when someone looks at something without the experience to judge it properly ("To an inexpert eye, the two paintings look identical, but a trained curator can tell the difference.")

Medicine:

"Inexpert use of surgical instruments can cause serious harm to a patient."

Music:

"Even an inexpert listener could tell the performer had not practised enough — the rhythm was uneven throughout."

Cooking:

"The sauce was an inexpert attempt at a classic French recipe — too thick, too salty, and missing depth."

Writing:

"The article was written in an inexpert way, jumping between ideas without any clear thread."

DIY/Home Repairs:

"The tiles were laid by someone inexpert at the job — several were cracked and none of them were level."

• Unskilled — the most direct synonym; plain and simple
  • Amateurish — done without professional skill, often implying it looks like a beginner did it
  • Clumsy — lacking coordination or care, though this also carries a physical sense
  • Inept — lacking skill, often implying the person is poorly suited for the task
  • Unpractised — not having practiced enough to be good at something

• Expert — the direct opposite; highly skilled and knowledgeable
  • Skilled — having well-developed ability
  • Proficient — competent and capable, above average
  • Adept — very skilled, smooth, and natural at something
  • Masterful — performing with the authority and ease of a master
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

Inexpert = not skilled enough. It describes a person, action, or result that falls short of the standard a truly skilled person would meet — not out of laziness or stupidity, but simply because the expertise isn't there yet (or hasn't developed fully).
8738: Something that is inexpiable is so terribly wrong — so deeply sinful or harmful — that it can never be fully atoned for, made right, or forgiven, no matter what is done to correct it.

To really understand "inexpiable," you first need to understand what atonement (or expiation) means. When someone does something wrong, they often try to make up for it — by apologizing sincerely, by accepting punishment, by doing good deeds to compensate, or by suffering the consequences of what they did. This process of making amends, of balancing out a wrongdoing, is called atonement or expiation.

Now, "inexpiable" says: that process is impossible here. The wrong is so enormous, so irreversible, or so deeply evil that nothing can ever fully repair it. No punishment is sufficient. No apology is enough. No good deed can balance it out. The weight of it simply cannot be lifted.

The word is almost always used in a moral or spiritual context. It typically describes:

1. Sins or crimes of extreme gravity
These are wrongs so monstrous that human or even divine justice struggles to fully account for them. Think of the deliberate slaughter of innocent people, the betrayal of someone who trusted you completely, or acts of cruelty so severe they leave a permanent scar on the world.

Example: "The warlord's massacre of the village was an inexpiable crime — no punishment in the world could give back what was taken."

2. Guilt that cannot be washed away
Sometimes a person carries guilt so heavy that even after they are punished, even after they confess, even after decades of trying to do good — they still feel the stain of what they did. That guilt can be described as inexpiable because it resists being erased.

Example: "She spent her whole life doing charity work, but the inexpiable guilt of her past betrayal never truly left her."

3. Hatred or enmity that cannot be appeased
Less commonly, "inexpiable" is also used to describe hatred or conflict that is so deep-rooted it can never be satisfied, settled, or resolved. Think of two enemies whose hatred is so profound that no peace deal, no passage of time, and no gesture of goodwill can cool it.

Example: "The two families had an inexpiable hatred for each other — generations of bloodshed had made reconciliation unthinkable."
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Inexpiable" is an extremely heavy word. It carries a sense of finality and hopelessness about the possibility of moral repair. When you call something inexpiable, you are not just saying it was bad — you are saying it exists beyond the reach of any redemptive process. It is a word that conveys despair, gravity, and moral condemnation all at once.

Because of this weight, you would not casually use it for ordinary mistakes or everyday wrongdoings. You would not say "forgetting your friend's birthday is inexpiable." The word belongs in contexts where the stakes are the highest — where we are talking about the deepest violations of human dignity, conscience, or trust.

It is important not to confuse "inexpiable" with the similar-sounding word "inexplicable," which means something that cannot be explained. These two words are completely different in meaning:

  • Inexplicable → cannot be explained ("Her sudden disappearance was inexplicable.")
  • Inexpiable → cannot be atoned for ("His cruelty toward the innocent was inexpiable.")

Synonyms (words with a similar meaning):

  • Unpardonable — cannot be pardoned or forgiven
  • Unforgivable — beyond forgiveness
  • Irremediable — cannot be remedied or fixed
  • Irredeemable — beyond the possibility of being redeemed
  • Implacable — (when used of hatred) cannot be appeased or softened

Antonyms (words with the opposite meaning):

  • Expiable — capable of being atoned for
  • Pardonable — capable of being forgiven
  • Redeemable — capable of being redeemed or made right

"Inexpiable" is a formal, literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in serious writing — philosophy, theology, classical literature, or grave moral discourse — than in everyday conversation. If you use it in speech, it will immediately signal that you are speaking with great seriousness and gravity. It is not a casual word.
Inexpiable = so deeply wrong that no punishment, apology, or good deed can ever fully make it right.
8739:
Something is inexplicable when it cannot be explained — not just when it hasn't been explained yet, but when no satisfying explanation seems to exist, or when every attempt to explain it falls short.

Think of it this way: if something strange happens and someone asks "Why did that happen?" — and the only honest answer is "I don't know, and I'm not sure anyone can know" — that thing is inexplicable.
Breaking It Down Intuitively

The word is built from a simple logic:

  • "Explicable" = something that can be explained
  • "In-" = a prefix meaning not
  • So "inexplicable" = something that cannot be explained

It's the same logic as visible → invisible, or capable → incapable.
The Important Nuance

This is where most learners stop, but understanding the full flavor of this word is what makes you use it like a native speaker.

"Inexplicable" carries a feeling of genuine puzzlement or wonder. It's not a neutral word. When you call something inexplicable, you're suggesting that it goes beyond ordinary confusion — it resists logic, reason, or any framework you have available.

There are two main situations where people use it:

1. Something is objectively mysterious — no scientific or logical explanation exists (or has been found), even after careful investigation.

The disappearance of the entire crew remained inexplicable — no storm, no wreckage, no distress signal.

2. Someone's behavior or choice seems so irrational that no sensible reason can account for it — even if there might be a reason hidden somewhere.

She had inexplicable hatred for the color blue. Nobody, including herself, could explain it.

The second use is very common in everyday life. When someone does something that baffles you completely — something that seems to defy reason — you call it inexplicable.
Sentences That Show It in Action

These examples are arranged from simple to more complex so you can see the range of how the word lives in real language.

  • His fear of butterflies was completely inexplicable.
  • The machine stopped working for no inexplicable reason. ❌ (This is wrong — see the "Common Mistake" section below.)
  • The machine stopped working for an inexplicable reason. ✓
  • There was an inexplicable silence in the room after he spoke.
  • Doctors were troubled by the patient's inexplicable recovery.
  • She felt an inexplicable sadness every time she passed that old building.
  • The connection between the two strangers felt inexplicable, as if they had known each other for years.
How It Sits in a Sentence

"Inexplicable" is a regular adjective, so it behaves exactly like other adjectives.

Before a noun:

an inexplicable event / an inexplicable feeling / an inexplicable choice

After a linking verb (is, was, seemed, remained, felt, appeared):

The outcome was inexplicable. / His behavior seemed inexplicable. / The case remained inexplicable.
The Adverb Form: Inexplicably

The adverb "inexplicably" is just as common and important to know. It means "in a way that cannot be explained" and modifies verbs and adjectives.

He inexplicably quit his dream job the day after getting it.
The lights inexplicably went out for exactly one minute, then came back on.
She was inexplicably drawn to places she had never been.

"Inexplicably" is especially powerful when the action it describes is surprising or jarring, because it signals to the reader: pay attention — this doesn't make sense on the surface.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

Knowing nearby words sharpens your understanding of exactly what "inexplicable" means.

Unexplainable — essentially the same meaning, but less formal. In casual speech, people often say "unexplainable" where a writer might choose "inexplicable."

Mysterious — suggests something hidden, secret, or unknown. A mysterious thing could have an explanation that is simply concealed. An inexplicable thing resists explanation even when nothing is hidden.

Baffling — emphasizes your own confusion. A baffling thing confuses you deeply. An inexplicable thing has no explanation, full stop — whether it confuses you or not.

Puzzling — milder than inexplicable. A puzzling thing is confusing and strange, but there's still a sense that an explanation might be around the corner. An inexplicable thing goes further — it feels beyond reach.

Incomprehensible — this means something cannot be understood, which is slightly different from cannot be explained. Something can be explained but still not understood (a complex equation), or understood but not explained (a gut feeling). "Inexplicable" is specifically about the inability to give a reason or account for something.
Words That Mean the Opposite

• Explicable — can be explained
  • Explainable — same as above, more informal
  • Understandable — makes sense, can be accounted for
  • Comprehensible — can be understood and grasped
A Common Mistake to Avoid

❌ "It stopped for no inexplicable reason."

This is a double negative error. "Inexplicable" already contains the idea of "no explanation." Adding "no" creates a contradiction — it accidentally means "it stopped for a reason that CAN be explained."

✅ "It stopped for an inexplicable reason."
✅ "It stopped for no explicable reason."

Both of these are correct. Choose one, not both.
Register and Tone

"Inexplicable" is a semi-formal to formal word. You'll find it comfortably in:

  • Literature and novels
  • Journalism and news writing
  • Academic and scientific writing
  • Thoughtful everyday conversation

It's not a word you'd typically hear in a very casual chat ("that's so weird / that makes no sense / I have no idea why"), but it's not so stiff that it sounds out of place when spoken. It sits comfortably in the middle — educated and precise, but not cold or overly technical.
The Feeling the Word Carries

This is the final layer, and it's what separates a learner from a fluent user.

"Inexplicable" often carries a trace of awe, unease, or wonder — the emotional texture of standing in front of something that your mind simply cannot grab hold of. It's the word you reach for when reason runs out. That's why it appears so often in stories about the supernatural, in descriptions of deep human emotion, and in accounts of events that leave investigators without answers.

When you call something inexplicable, you're not just saying "I don't know why." You're saying: "This thing sits outside the reach of easy explanation — and that matters."
